thread.title: Apple may have lost more than a third of its market share in China (AAPL)

author: sunmag.net
title: Apple may have lost more than a third of its market share in China (AAPL)
text:
Apple may have lost more than a third of its market share in China and up to half its share in major metropolitan areas. Analysts are describing the company's performance there as "weak." Many people in China may not be able to afford an iPhone. Though Apple now has a large base in China, a "supercycle" of upgrades keeps not happening. Competition from domestic Android-makers, like Huawei and Oppo, has been much stronger than expected. Apple's revenues in China in the first quarter increased by 11%, to $18 billion, and CEO Tim Cook told analysts in February, "Everywhere I look, I feel really good about how we're doing in China."
But researchers with sources in China aren't so bullish. They think the iPhone X may be hemmed in by its $1,000 price, which places it far out of reach of many consumers in China, and by the aggressiveness of local manufacturers such as Huawei.
The analysts forecast that Apple's China sales, which tend to cycle wildly from quarter to quarter, will soon decline. And they think Apple's market share may have been cut by one-third or more in the past three years. The China numbers will be closely watched on today's earnings call .&
Katy Huberty, an analyst at Morgan Stanley, says she sees "continued weakness in China" for the upcoming quarter, while analysts at UBS and Nomura also used the word "weak" to describe Apple's recent performance there.
The problem is that in 2015, when Apple launched the iPhone 6S, the company had a stellar year in China and Hong Kong. It sold 71 million phones in the region, according to data from UBS and Gartner.
That has been hard to beat. In Apple's fiscal 2017, that number was down to 49 million. The UBS analysts Steven Milunovich and Benjamin Wilson estimate that it will decline to 47 million in fiscal 2018.
Apple's iPhone unit sales in China: 2015: 71 million 2016: 59 million 2017: 49 million 2018 (estimate): 47 million Source: UBS estimates/Gartner "We think it's doubtful China returns to its 2015 peak as local brands have caught up and upgrade cycles are lengthening; we expect a flattish market, give or take a few points of growth depending on the overall market and product cycle," the UBS team recently told clients. "At the peak in 2015, we believe Apple likely had 40-50% share with Tier 1 and 2 consumers; we think that figure is closer to 20-30% today."
Morgan Stanley thinks Apple's share may be down to 18%, less than half of UBS's share estimate from 2015. Jeffrey Kvaal of Nomura has a similar view.
"Non-Chinese smartphone shipments in China, which are mostly iPhones, fell YoY in the month of March," Kvaal told clients. "C1Q shipments fell 9% YoY or 41% sequentially, below the 3-year seasonality of down 32%."
Total smartphone shipments and iPhone shipments are closely correlated, according to Kvaal's data.
The problem is that though China is a vast market, many people there are poor by Western standards. There are 1.3 billion people in China, but only about 200 million to 300 million of them live in the so-called Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities, like Shanghai or Beijing, that are generally rich enough to afford iPhones. Of those, only 220 million could possibly be Apple customers UBS believes. Outside those metro centers, Apple has few distributors and promoters.
"Local brands make extensive use of promoters to influence consumer decisions," Milunovich says. "Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei have over 100,000 promoters each versus Apple with only 4,000."
Meanwhile, Huawei and other high-end Android-makers have upped their game, accumulating a 56% share of the market to Apple's 37% today.& Back in 2015 it was Apple with the dominant share, at 54%, according to data from UBS and Gartner. That represents a collapse of 32 points in market share.
Since Apple's 2015 success, analysts have been eagerly awaiting a "supercycle" of upgrades as people swap their old iPhones for new ones. But that keeps not happening, partly because people are keeping their iPhones longer, and partly because Apple has launched new phones with features that are only marginal improvements over the older models.
"Patience is wearing thin among investors on this elusive upgrade cycle with China playing a major role in the success or failure Apple will see over the coming year around this key product upgrade cycle," Daniel Ives, a GBH Insights analyst, recently said in a research note.
